Differences: LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm and QKNorm

Differences 3 and 4 of 6

Transformer Blocks · LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm16

Layer Normalization: LayerNorm

Keeps every token's features on a stable scale

\green{y} = \frac{\blue{x} - \text{E}[\blue{x}]}{\sqrt{\text{Var}[\blue{x}] + \red{\epsilon}}} * \purple{\gamma} + \purple{\beta}
  • Scale drifts: residual adds pile up, so activations grow with depth
  • Stable inputs: huge values saturate softmax and kill gradients
  • Faster training: smoother loss, higher learning rates work
  • Per token, not per batch: same at train and inference, any batch size
  • γ, β: learned scale and shift keep the layer expressive
Transformer Blocks · LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm17

RMSNorm

A simpler LayerNorm that most modern LLMs use instead

\green{y} = \frac{\blue{x}}{\sqrt{\text{mean}(\blue{x}^2) + \red{\epsilon}}} * \purple{\gamma}
  • Drops centering: no mean subtraction, no β
  • Cheaper: one statistic instead of two
  • Same quality: rescaling matters more than recentering
Transformer Blocks · LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm18

QKNorm: RMSNorm on Q and K

Normalize each head's Q and K before the dot product, so attention scores can't blow up

q' = \frac{\blue{q}}{\sqrt{\text{mean}(\blue{q}^2) + \epsilon}} * \purple{\gamma_q}
  • Per head: RMSNorm over head_dim on Q and K
  • Why: stops |Q · K| from growing, so softmax can't saturate
  • Where: after the Q/K projections, before RoPE, V untouched
Transformer Blocks · LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm19

Differences: Positional Encoding vs. RoPE

Difference 5 of 6

Transformer Blocks · Positional Encoding vs. RoPE20

Positional Encodings

Attention is order-blind, so we add a position vector to each token

\text{PE}(pos, 2i) = \sin\bp{pos / 10000^{2i/d}} \text{PE}(pos, 2i+1) = \cos\bp{pos / 10000^{2i/d}}
Transformer Blocks · Positional Encoding vs. RoPE21

Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE)

Instead of transforming the embeddings themselves, we transform the Q and K matrices during attention calculations.

This is one of the trickiest things I've seen in the past few years

Differences: Dropout vs. No Dropout

Difference 6 of 6

Transformer Blocks · Dropout vs. No Dropout24

Dropout vs. No Dropout

Dropout randomly zeroes activations during training so the network can't rely on any single feature. It is only used during training!

  • Training only: fresh random mask each step, identity at inference
  • Rescale by 1/(1 − p): keeps the expected activation unchanged
  • Why: helps prevent overfitting

Dropout is used to fight overfitting. However, because modern LLMs are trained on such an insane scale of data and the data is so widely varied, overfitting is much less of a concern, so dropout isn't necessary.
